query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and evolution of coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) and their interaction with dislocations, which can be controlled by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with a face-centered cubic (FCC) or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure
generation.intervention: Introduction of stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) into the alloy
generation.conditions: High-temperature applications, such as plasma-facing components, with exposure to mechanical vibrations and stresses
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) and their interaction with dislocations
generation.mechanism: Dislocation transmission and relief of stress concentrations through the formation and evolution of SCCPs, leading to improved toughness and resistance to corrosion and oxidation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved toughness, strength, and ductility, as well as enhanced resistance to corrosion and oxidation, in high-entropy alloys with SCCPs
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 298-973 K, and exposure to mechanical vibrations and stresses
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms by which SCCPs interact with dislocations and influence the retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys, and the optimal conditions for the formation and evolution of SCCPs

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with high-entropy alloys with and without SCCPs, exposed to mechanical vibrations and stresses at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloys with SCCPs do not exhibit improved toughness, strength, and ductility, and enhanced resistance to corrosion and oxidation, compared to traditional high-entropy alloys without SCCPs, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .
